title.text:
Prompting and
reasoning models

objects.text: How do I get reliable work out of an assistant?

Applied AI and Automation  |  Session 8 of the 15 (Sessions 0 to 14)
KLAi Professional Learning  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes:
Welcome to Session 8. Last time we opened the model file and saw why size and licence decide whether you rent, host or own a model. Whichever route you choose, you still have to tell the model what you want, so our question today is: how do I get reliable work out of an assistant?

We build it from what you already know about next-token prediction, then add one prompt technique at a time, each with a recorded before and after, and then learn to test a prompt with numbers.

slides.notes:
That question gives you three things to be able to do. You can explain why a prompt changes the answer, and write a prompt with five parts. You can ask for a table or JSON so the answer can be checked. And you can score prompts on an evaluation set, and say what to expect from a reasoning model.

The checking matters as much as the writing, because a confident answer can still be wrong.

title.text:
Your two hours: why prompts work, five
parts, testing, then your own prompt

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_plan_11.90x3.95_c0a59e81.png
objects.alt: The two hours in parts, in minutes

objects.text: Fifty minutes of ideas with recorded before-and-after runs, then a weak prompt rewritten on paper.

slides.notes:
To get you there, the two hours have a clear order. After the recall, fifty minutes on the ideas: why a prompt changes the answer at all, then the five parts of a prompt, each with a recorded before and after, then how to test a prompt on an evaluation set, and what a reasoning model does differently.

Twenty minutes go to the larger recorded demonstrations, including a payroll sum that one prompt got wrong. After the break you have twenty minutes to rewrite a weak prompt on paper, and ten to choose which of your own prompts to test first.

title.text: Three questions from last time

runs.text: 1.  What is the difference between open source and open weights?
2.  How big is the weights file of a model with 7 billion parameters at FP16?
3.  Is GGUF a file format or a level of precision?

objects.text: Answer aloud first. Then we check together.

slides.notes:
Three quick questions from Session 7. Answer aloud first, and then we check together. 

Question one. What is the difference between open source and open weights? Take a moment.

A good answer is this. Open weights means the trained parameters can be downloaded, under a licence that may still limit use. Open Source AI in the OSI sense also needs the training code, information about the training data and a licence without use limits.

Question two. How big is the weights file of a model with 7 billion parameters at FP16? Say it to yourself first.

A good answer is this. About 14 GB. Parameters times bytes per parameter, which is 2 bytes at FP16, with working memory needed on top.

Question three. Is GGUF a file format or a level of precision? Think about your own work as you answer.

A good answer is this. A file format. The number of bits per parameter is a separate choice called quantisation, and a GGUF file can hold FP16 or 4-bit parameters.

If an answer was missing, last session’s take-away sheet has it.

title.text: Words we use today

rows.text: The prompt is all the text you give a model. A system prompt holds standing instructions; a user prompt is this request.
Zero-shot prompting gives only the instruction. Few-shot prompting adds a few worked examples (shots) first.
An answer in fixed named fields. JSON is a plain-text format of named fields that a program can read.
An evaluation set is test cases with known right answers. Accuracy = correct answers ÷ total cases.
Chain-of-thought asks the model to write its steps. A reasoning model writes its own working before it answers.

slides.notes:
Five words for today. We use every one of them before the end of the session.

Prompt, system prompt. The prompt is all the text you give a model. A system prompt holds standing instructions; a user prompt is this request.

Zero-shot, few-shot. Zero-shot prompting gives only the instruction. Few-shot prompting adds a few worked examples (shots) first.

Structured output, JSON. An answer in fixed named fields. JSON is a plain-text format of named fields that a program can read.

Evaluation set, accuracy. An evaluation set is test cases with known right answers. Accuracy = correct answers ÷ total cases.

Chain-of-thought, reasoning model. Chain-of-thought asks the model to write its steps. A reasoning model writes its own working before it answers.

title.text:
A language model writes by predicting the
next token, again and again, as in Session 5

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t08_loop_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: A language model writes by predicting the next token, again and again, as in Session 5

objects.text: A token is a word or part of a word. The model gives every possible next token a probability.

runs.text: A probability is a share of 100%: 30.4% means about 30 times in 100.
One token is picked and added, and the loop repeats.

slides.notes:
Before we write a single prompt, we need to know why the wording of a prompt changes the answer at all, and the reason is something you met in Session 5. A language model reads text as tokens, words or parts of words. For the text so far, it gives every token in its vocabulary a probability, a share of one hundred percent.

In this real GPT-2 run, after thank you for your, the token support got 30.4 percent, continued 10.3 and patience 5.4, and fifty thousand others shared the rest. One token is picked, added to the text, and the loop goes round again. Assistants are post-trained to follow instructions, as in Session 6, but they still write this way, one token after another, starting from your prompt.

title.text:
Your prompt is the start of that text, so
it changes which next tokens are likely

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t08_continues_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Your prompt is the start of that text, so it changes which next tokens are likely

objects.text: The model continues whatever you write. More detail leaves fewer likely next tokens.

runs.text: Loose start: the ten likeliest tokens add up to only 42%.
Tight start: the top three add up to 97%.

slides.notes:
Your prompt is the text so far. Everything the model writes is a continuation of it, so every word you add changes the probabilities of what comes next. A taxi driver told take me to town has hundreds of places to choose from. Take me to Garden City, main entrance, leaves one.

These two lists are real, from the same small model. After the capital of Uganda is, the ten likeliest tokens add up to only forty-two percent. After please pay the invoice within thirty, the top three add up to ninety-seven percent; the bracket leads because invoices often write the number twice, thirty, then 30 in brackets; after it, the model puts 99 percent on 30.

A prompt technique is a way of adding text that narrows the choice. One more thing from Session 5 affects which token is picked: the temperature.

title.text:
Temperature divides each logit by
T before softmax, as in Session 5

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t08_tempformula_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Temperature divides each logit by T before softmax, as in Session 5

objects.text: Logits 3, 2 and 0 from the Session 5 hands-on. Low T repeats; high T varies. One run proves little.

slides.notes:
Your Session 5 hands-on numbers show how it works. The model gives each token a raw score, a logit, written z. Softmax turns the scores into probabilities: raise e, about 2.72, to each score, add the results, and divide each by the total. At T equal to 1, e to the 3, the 2 and the 0 are 20.09, 7.39 and 1, the total is 28.47, so 70.5, 25.9 and 3.5 percent.

Temperature T divides each logit first. At T equal to 2, 4.48, 2.72 and 1 give 54.7, 33.1 and 12.2 percent, a flatter spread. In words: probability of token i equals e to its logit over T, divided by the sum of the same for every token. Because a token is drawn by chance, the same prompt can give a different reply next time.

title.text:
A vague prompt leaves the model to guess;
five parts of a prompt remove five guesses

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t08_brief_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: A vague prompt leaves the model to guess; five parts of a prompt remove five guesses

objects.text: Each part of a prompt answers one question the model would otherwise guess.

runs.text: Everyday case: asking an assistant for a dinner recipe.
Next: a recorded before and after for each part.

slides.notes:
So a prompt narrows the next tokens, and a vague one leaves the model to fill gaps with whatever is most likely in general. Take a dinner request. Ask, make dinner, and the model must guess five things. Who is speaking and at what level: the role. What your situation is: the context.

Which labels and layout you want: examples. How long and what shape: the format. And what is off limits, or what to do when unsure: the constraints. Instructions to a new colleague on day one work the same way; that is an analogy, and the colleague, like the model, knows nothing about your family or your company.

We take the parts one at a time, each with a real run before and after.

title.text:
Naming a role changes the voice
and the level of the answer

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t08_ba_role_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Naming a role changes the voice and the level of the answer

objects.text: Recorded: Claude fresh subagents, 11 November 2026, one run each. Not ChatGPT or Gemini.

slides.notes:
The first guess is the voice and the level. On the left, I asked a fresh assistant to explain inflation in at most sixty words, with no role. The answer was right, and written for an economist: a price index, the money supply. On the right, the only change is one sentence: you are a primary school teacher talking to a class of ten-year-olds.

The reply became a chocolate bar that costs 1,000 shillings today and 1,200 next year. Same idea, different level. A role adds no facts. It shifts which words are likely, because text written by teachers for children continues differently from text written by economists. Each pair is one run, so it shows the effect and proves no rate. Next, the situation.

title.text:
Context about your situation
makes the answer fit your case

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t08_ba_context_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Context about your situation makes the answer fit your case

objects.text: Recorded runs, 11 November 2026, one each. The extras show why constraints are the fifth part.

slides.notes:
The second guess is your situation. With no context, suggest a dinner I can cook tonight gave a lemon-garlic chicken stir-fry with broccoli and snap peas. A fine dish, but the model could not know that one of us is vegetarian or what is in the kitchen. On the right I added four people, one vegetarian, beans, rice, tomatoes and onions at home, and forty-five minutes.

Now it suggested a bean and tomato stew over rice in about thirty-five minutes. The last line, though, still added cumin, paprika and an optional egg, which I never mentioned. Context makes the answer fit; it does not stop additions. That is a job for constraints, which we reach in a moment. First, examples.

title.text:
Examples (few-shot): show two finished cases,
so the model copies the labels and layout

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t08_ba_fewshot_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Examples (few-shot): show two finished cases, so the model copies the labels and layout

objects.text: Zero-shot: instruction alone. Few-shot: worked examples (shots) first. Recorded, 11 Nov 2026.

slides.notes:
The third guess is the exact labels and layout. Zero-shot prompting gives only the instruction. I asked for labels on three mobile money messages and got right answers in the model’s own words: money in, received, money out, bill payment, plus totals nobody asked for, seventy-three words. Few-shot prompting puts finished examples, called shots, before the new case.

With two shots labelled IN and OUT, the reply was one word per line: IN, OUT, IN. Why does it work?

The shots are part of the text the model continues, so the likeliest next tokens copy their pattern. Google’s guide advises varied examples in one layout, and warns that too many alike can overfit, the idea from Sessions 0 and 2 of fitting the examples too closely.

title.text:
A stated format turned a 529-word
answer into a three-row table

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t08_ba_format_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: A stated format turned a 529-word answer into a three-row table

objects.text: Recorded runs, 11 November 2026, one run each. Words counted with a standard tool.

slides.notes:
The fourth guess is how long and what shape. Compare renting and buying a house, with no format, gave 529 words under seven headings, with rules of thumb and advice to see a financial adviser. Nothing wrong, but you cannot compare two options at a glance in 529 words.

The only change on the right is the format: answer only with a table, two columns, three rows, at most eight words a cell. The reply was that table and nothing else. A stated format also makes the answer easy to check: you can see at once whether a row is missing.

Four guesses are now gone. One is left: what the model must not do. Remember the dinner run, which added cumin and an egg.

title.text:
Constraints set what is off limits
and what to say when unsure

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t08_ba_constraints_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Constraints set what is off limits and what to say when unsure

objects.text: Recorded runs, 11 November 2026, one each. Before is the context run from earlier.

slides.notes:
The fifth guess is the limits. Constraints are the rules the answer must keep: what the model must not do, and what to say when it is unsure. On the left is the context run you saw two slides ago. It fitted our evening, and still added garlic, cumin, paprika and an egg we never mentioned.

On the right I added two sentences: use only the ingredients I listed, plus salt, oil and water, and if a good dish needs anything else, say so. The reply kept to the list. It named garlic, chili or cumin as improvements we had not listed, and it warned that forty-five minutes holds only if the beans are canned or precooked.

A constraint does not add knowledge. It sets the edges, and invites the model to say what it lacks.

title.text:
The same sales data, sent once with a
weak prompt and once with a strong one

objects.text: I will show

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t08_briefs_7.30x3.90.png
objects.alt: The same sales data, sent once with a weak prompt and once with a strong one

objects.text: Watch for

runs.text: Recorded runs, Claude fresh subagent sessions, 4 November 2026. Not ChatGPT or Gemini.
Both runs got the figures right.
Only the strong prompt said what the data cannot explain.

slides.notes:
You have seen each part alone on everyday tasks. Now the parts together on a real business task, where the constraints matter most. Each Monday, Nile Valley Foods, or NVF, our case company, which sells maize flour, sugar and cooking oil, sends its Sales Director a short email with last week’s sales.

Both prompts gave the same data. The weak one said only, write the Monday sales email. The strong one named the role and the reader, set the format, and added constraints: use only these figures, and admit what the data cannot explain. In both, the figures came out right.

The weak run added advice to keep beans and sugar in stock, which nobody asked for, and left a blank where your name should go. The strong run followed the format and ended with one thing to check.

title.text:
The strong prompt had four of
the five parts and no example

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t08_fivepart_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: The strong prompt had four of the five parts and no example

objects.text: The strong prompt from the recorded run. It had no example. Add one when the format matters.

slides.notes:
So what made the strong one strong?

Here it is taken apart into the five parts you have now seen one by one. The role: you are the sales analyst. The context: who reads it. The examples are missing in this prompt; when the format matters, paste one finished email and say, write the next one like this.

The format: a subject line, a two-sentence summary, a table, at most three plain sentences. The constraints: use only these figures, do not invent a number, cause or customer, and say so if something cannot be explained. On examples, Anthropic and Google list them among their advice. OpenAI says to try its reasoning models with none first. All three stress clear instructions and a stated format.

title.text:
The system prompt holds standing rules,
and the user prompt holds this request

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t08_roles_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: The system prompt holds standing rules, and the user prompt holds this request

objects.text: The model reads both as one text to continue. Chat apps usually show only the user prompt.

slides.notes:
Now that you know the five parts, where do they go?

Most assistants take two kinds of prompt. The system prompt holds standing instructions that apply to every conversation: usually the role and the constraints, such as the language and the limits. The user prompt is what a person types for this request: the context, the data and the format for this job.

A restaurant works the same way: house rules given to the waiter at the start of the shift, then each customer’s order. At NVF the system prompt says you are the customer-service assistant, answer in English and never promise a refund. The user prompt is a message about leaking jerrycans. The model reads both together as one text to continue.

title.text:
Delimiters mark where the data starts
and ends, apart from the instructions

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t08_delims_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Delimiters mark where the data starts and ends, apart from the instructions

objects.text: A delimiter is a marker such as ### that shows where pasted data starts and ends.

runs.text: Like a cover sheet on a folder: instructions, then the papers.
A delimiter does not make the data safe.

slides.notes:
Once you paste data into a prompt, such as messages to label, the model has to tell your instructions from the data. In an office, a cover sheet says what to do and a folder holds the papers. In a prompt you build the same structure with delimiters, markers that show where one part ends and another begins.

The instructions come first. Then a line such as three hash signs and SMS start, then the data, then SMS end. OpenAI’s guide suggests markers like these, or tags in angle brackets. They help the model see where the data is. They do not make it safe: a message can contain an order, and the model may follow it.

That is called prompt injection, and we return to it in Sessions 10 and 11. Delimiters tidy what goes in; next, a way to tidy what comes out.

title.text:
JSON writes an answer as named fields
that a program can read one by one

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t08_jsonparts_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: JSON writes an answer as named fields that a program can read one by one

objects.text: Structured output: an answer in fixed named fields. JSON is a common format for it.

slides.notes:
A table suits a person, but a program cannot read a paragraph the way you do. JSON is written like an order slip with fixed boxes. Curly brackets hold one record, a set of named fields. Each field is a name in quotes, a colon, then its value: table, 4.

Square brackets hold a list, here the two items, and each item is a small record of its own, a dish and a quantity. Text values sit in quotes, and the word null means the field is empty. JSON stands for JavaScript Object Notation, and despite the name almost any program can read it.

Asking the model for an answer in fixed fields like these is called structured output.

title.text:
Structured output: ask for JSON, and every
reply comes back with the same fields

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t08_ba_json_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Structured output: ask for JSON, and every reply comes back with the same fields

objects.text: Recorded runs, 11 November 2026, one each. A program read the JSON reply without error.

slides.notes:
The restaurant order makes a good before and after. Asked to write the order down for the kitchen, the model gave a neat slip: kitchen order, table 4, two chapati, one tea with no sugar. A cook can use it, but a program cannot rely on it, because next time the layout may differ.

On the right I named the fields: return JSON only, with table as a number, items as a list of dish and quantity, and note as text or null. The reply had those fields and no others, and a short program read it without error. That is the value of structured output: the shape can be checked by a program, every time. Now the same idea on a real business task.

title.text:
Four real-looking customer messages
came back as four records with fixed fields

objects.text: I will show

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t08_structured_7.30x3.90.png
objects.alt: Four real-looking customer messages came back as four records with fixed fields

objects.text: Watch for

runs.text: Recorded run, Claude fresh subagent, 6 November 2026. One run.
Four messages came back as four records with fixed fields.
The highlighted fields are the type and the urgency.

slides.notes:
The same idea works on a business task, with the four messages listed after the instructions. This is a recorded run, and I want you to look at the type and the urgency in the highlighted fields. I gave the assistant four invented customer messages from NVF and a list of exact fields: customer, type, items, amount, urgency and reference.

The prompt said, use only what the message says, and use null if a field is missing. This is message three, the leaking jerrycans. The record names the type as complaint, the six unusable jerrycans, and the urgency as high. The customer is null, because the message gave no name.

Because the format is fixed, the reply can be checked field by field.

title.text:
A program checked the shape;
a person found two loose fields

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t08_checkgrid_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: A program checked the shape; a person found two loose fields

objects.text: Fix to try: split the reference into invoice number and payment reference, then run again.

slides.notes:
I checked the reply in two ways. A short program confirmed that it was valid JSON, meaning it follows the writing rules you saw, with four records and the fields I asked for, no more and no fewer. Then I read each field against the message. Everything matched except two.

For message one, the customer came back as the name and the shop together in one field. For message two, the invoice number and the mobile money reference came back joined, because my prompt allowed only one reference field. The fault lies in my prompt, and the reply did what it was told.

The cure is to split the field and run again. A format check catches the shape, and a person still checks the meaning. Deciding that one prompt is better than another takes more than one run.

title.text:
To compare prompts, score them on an
evaluation set: accuracy = correct ÷ total

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t08_evalset_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: To compare prompts, score them on an evaluation set: accuracy = correct ÷ total

objects.text: Evaluation set: test cases with known right answers. Run each prompt on all of them, and count.

slides.notes:
One good reply can be luck, because the next token is drawn by chance. So we test a prompt the way you would test a new cashier. Give ten bills whose totals you already know; those ten cases and their answers are the evaluation set. The cashier gets nine right; bill seven was written as 23,000 against a correct 23,500.

Count: nine correct, ten in total. Divide: nine divided by ten is 0.9, which is ninety percent. That is the accuracy of Session 3, and a Session 6 benchmark works the same way; an evaluation set is your own small benchmark. Higher is better. Watch small sets: one right out of two is fifty percent, three of three is one hundred, and one case more or less moves them a lot.

title.text:
Across four prompts, nine of ten
recorded payroll runs were right

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t08_payroll_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Across four prompts, nine of ten recorded payroll runs were right

objects.text: Accuracy = correct ÷ total. All ten runs: 9 ÷ 10 = 90%. Ten runs show a pattern and prove nothing.

slides.notes:
The same scoring works on a calculation. Payroll is the pay for the month: salary, plus overtime, minus an unpaid leave day, then minus pension and an advance; the net pay is what reaches the bank, and the right answer is 1,802,898 shillings, checked twice. The total cost to NVF, the gross pay plus its ten percent employer pension, should be 2,261,250.

Plain means the facts and a question. Framed means the goal, the rules and the output format are stated first. Re-add means one closing sentence: check your answer by re-adding the lines. Plain: one of two right, fifty percent. Plain plus re-add: three of three. Framed without it: three of three.

Framed with it: two of two. All ten: nine of ten, ninety percent. Ten runs cannot say which change helped. The one wrong run is worth a closer look.

title.text:
The wrong plain run was 200,000 out,
showed every line and sounded sure

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t08_slip_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: The wrong plain run was 200,000 out, showed every line and sounded sure

objects.text: Re-add it yourself: 1,800,000 plus 337,500 minus 81,818.

runs.text: The key gives 2,055,682.
Plain run 2 wrote 1,855,682.
Re-add the lines that matter.

slides.notes:
This is the wrong run, line by line. Every step was shown and the tone was calm. But the gross pay, the pay before deductions, added up to 1,855,682, and the right figure is 2,055,682. A slip of 200,000 shillings, and every figure after it was wrong. The net pay came out 190,000 short, because the five percent employee pension shrank with the gross.

You can catch this in a minute with a calculator: salary 1,800,000, plus overtime 337,500, minus the leave deduction 81,818. That is the habit. Ask for the working so you can check it, and recompute the figure that everything else depends on. A calm tone and shown working do not prove a sum is right.

title.text:
Keep a prompt log: write, run on the
evaluation set, score, change one thing

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t08_promptlog_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Keep a prompt log: write, run on the evaluation set, score, change one thing

objects.text: Accuracy = correct ÷ total. Two runs is a small set; a real evaluation set has ten cases or more.

slides.notes:
That is the habit for one reply. Across many replies, the habit is a loop, and it is how you improve a prompt. Write the prompt, run it on the evaluation set, score the answers against the key, change one thing, and run again, as you would test a new supplier.

Anthropic’s guide says to define success criteria and a way to test them before refining. Keep a log. Mine shows the payroll prompt plain and framed, with two runs each, and the orders prompt with one run. In the right column, one of two is fifty percent, two of two is one hundred.

Two runs is a small set, and a real evaluation set has ten or more cases. Start with a task where you already know the right answers.

title.text:
Chain-of-thought prompting asks the model
to write its steps, so you can check them

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t08_cot_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Chain-of-thought prompting asks the model to write its steps, so you can check them

objects.text: Chain-of-thought: you ask for the steps. A reasoning model, next, writes such steps by itself.

slides.notes:
The payroll slip leads to the last group of ideas: models that write out their working. Chain-of-thought prompting means you ask the model to write its reasoning steps before the final answer. Take a shop bill: three kilograms of sugar at 4,500 shillings and two kilograms of rice at 5,000.

An answer-only reply gives one number you must trust. With chain-of-thought each line is written, 13,500 plus 10,000 is 23,500, so you can check each multiplication and the addition. Why can it help?

Each written step becomes part of the text the model continues, so later tokens build on it. Published work found it often helps on multi-step problems, and it guarantees nothing. The bill on the slide is an illustration only. Reasoning models do this on their own.

title.text:
A reasoning model writes working tokens first,
which is slower and often better on many steps

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t08_reasoning_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: A reasoning model writes working tokens first, which is slower and often better on many steps

objects.text: What you see and what vendors publish. We make no claim about how closed products work inside.

slides.notes:
In Session 6 you met reasoning models, trained to write a long stretch of working before the answer. Here is what is different for you. A standard model starts the answer straight away. A reasoning model, or an assistant with its thinking switched on, first writes working tokens, then the answer.

Depending on the product, you see the working, a summary of it, or nothing. What to expect: it is slower, and the working is made of tokens, which usually count towards the bill. It can do better on problems with many steps, like the payroll sum, and it can still be wrong, so you still check.

I make no claim about how any closed product does this inside. I did not record a reasoning model against a standard one; we try that live shortly.

title.text:
The vendor guides agree on stating
the goal and the limits, then testing

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t08_vendors_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: The vendor guides agree on stating the goal and the limits, then testing

objects.text: Guides read on 6 November 2026. Product names and settings change often.

slides.notes:
So how should you prompt a reasoning model?

Each vendor answers in its own terms, and I add nothing. OpenAI’s guide for its reasoning models says to use short, direct prompts, and that asking for step-by-step reasoning is unnecessary and can sometimes hurt. Anthropic says its models can think before answering, and that newer models decide how much thinking to do, with an effort setting you can raise or lower.

Google says its Gemini thinking models reason on their own, so you usually need not ask for steps. On testing they agree in spirit: a precise goal, success criteria, and iterate. So for a reasoning model, frame the problem: state the goal, the rules and the output, and leave the working to it.

title.text:
Live, the same payroll prompt
with thinking off and then on

objects.text: I will show

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_flow_7.30x3.90_b02120ae.png
objects.alt: Live, the same payroll prompt with thinking off and then on

objects.text: Watch for

runs.text: Live, on your assistant. Results vary from run to run.
Time taken and the length of the answer.
Whether the net pay matches the key.

slides.notes:
Time to see it, live, on the assistant you use, and nothing here is recorded. Many assistants have a switch that lets the model think longer. I paste the same framed payroll prompt twice, once with thinking off and once with it on. Watch the time each takes and the length of the answer, and then I compare the net pay with the key, 1,802,898.

Results vary from run to run, as the temperature slide showed, so one try proves nothing; it is one case of an evaluation set. If your assistant has no such switch, we use the recorded runs instead. Whatever the result, the final step is the same: you check the figure that matters.

title.text:
Which kind of model to start
with depends on the task

rows.text: Well defined and quick; OpenAI says fast, defined tasks suit standard models
Extra working can help; you still re-add the lines
Anything with money, law or people
Our plain run was wrong with every line shown

objects.text: A starting view. Test it on your own evaluation set, and ask your IT lead what the thinking costs.

slides.notes:
What did you see with thinking on and off?

Whatever it was, it leads to the question of which model to start with, and this is a starting view that you test. For well-defined jobs such as sorting messages, rewriting or a short summary, start with a standard model. OpenAI’s guide says fast, well-defined work suits its standard models, and that planning and ambiguous complex problems suit its reasoning models.

For multi-step sums, plans or tangled rules, turn thinking on, and still re-add the lines. And for anything involving money, law or people, either kind, followed by a check by hand. Our own plain run was wrong with every line shown. Ask your IT lead what thinking costs on the plan you use.

title.text:
Improve a weak prompt
with the five-part checklist

objects.text: 20 minutes
Hands-on, no computer
Rewrite the weak prompt: "Reply to this customer complaint."

runs.text: Name the role and the reader.
Add the context: what happened, which customer.
Add one example, or write "none yet".
State the format and length.
Add the constraints, and what to say when unsure.

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_sheet_5.50x3.55_416a2d35.png
objects.alt: What your finished page looks like

objects.text: You keep: A rewritten prompt, checked against all five parts, ready for your log.

slides.notes:
Time for you to use the checklist. This part is on paper, with no computer, and you have twenty minutes. Take the weak prompt on the slide, reply to this customer complaint, and rewrite it using the five parts, as each before and after did. Name the role and the reader.

Add the context: what happened and which customer. Add one example, or write none yet. State the format and the length. Add the constraints and what to say if the assistant is unsure. Then read your prompt aloud as if you were the new colleague. What would you still have to guess?

If your own work gives a better case, use that. I will come round and read your drafts.

title.text:
Which of your prompts will
you test first, and how?

objects.text: Which prompt do you use often enough to test properly?

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_pin_0.80.png
objects.alt: pin

objects.text: Save it
Write it in the prompt template.

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_check_0.80.png
objects.alt: check

objects.text: Test it
Run it on an evaluation set of ten cases.

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_chart_0.80.png
objects.alt: chart

objects.text: Structure it
Ask for a table or JSON so it can be checked.

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_shield_0.80.png
objects.alt: shield

objects.text: Keep a person
Name who checks the figures before use.
Write the prompt, the first test and who checks it.

slides.notes:
You have rewritten one prompt, so now turn to the prompts you use every week. Pick the one you use most often. Will you save it in the template?

Will you test it on an evaluation set of ten cases where you know the right answer, and work out its accuracy?

Will you ask for a table or JSON so that the answer can be checked?

Or will you name the person who checks the figures before anything is used?

Most prompts need two or three of these. Write down the prompt, the first test you will run, and who does the check. I would like to hear two or three of your choices, with what each prompt could get wrong.

title.text:
Today’s five-part checklist fits inside
the seven-part prompt template

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t08_template_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Today’s five-part checklist fits inside the seven-part prompt template

objects.text: Templates/Reusable Brief Template.docx (the file keeps its old name). Examples go with the inputs.

slides.notes:
Whichever you chose, all of it needs one place to live, and you already have it. The reusable prompt template has seven parts. The five-part checklist from today fits inside it. The goal and context cover the role and the context. Output format is the format, and constraints are the constraints.

It adds three things, shown in red. Inputs list what you give the assistant, and that is also where an example goes. How I will check says how you will test the answer on your evaluation set. And what to say when unsure is the cheapest guard against an invented answer.

Use the template, and record each version and its accuracy in your prompt log. Those two are what you keep today.

title.text:
Keep the template and the log,
and test every prompt you reuse

objects.text: What you keep from today

runs.text: A reusable prompt template and a prompt log, so that every prompt you keep has been tested on an evaluation set.

Reliable work comes from a clear prompt, an evaluation set and a person who checks the figure that matters.

Test every prompt before you reuse it. Next session is about giving a model your own knowledge: retrieval-augmented generation, long context and fine-tuning. Bring one question that needs your own documents.

We began with this question: How do I get reliable work out of an assistant? Before you go, say in one sentence what you can now say about it.
